result: The TIRF-based supported bilayer/liposome assay can distinguish sequential steps in membrane fusion (tethering, docking, hemifusion, and content release) with single-particle resolution and kinetic information.
evaluation: Claims C32-C39 describe the methodological capabilities of the TIRF assay. The assay design is well-documented with appropriate controls and reporters (TexasRed for lipid mixing, calcein for content release). The method provides advantages over bulk measurements (C34) and captures kinetic data (C35), which are validated through the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

result: Human l-Opa1 and s-Opa1 were successfully purified from Pichia pastoris and reconstituted into lipid bilayers and liposomes with validated GTPase activity and proper membrane integration.
evaluation: Claims C40-C59 describe protein purification and reconstitution validation. Multiple orthogonal methods confirm successful reconstitution: GTPase activity assays (C42-C43), co-flotation analysis (C48, C125-C131), FCS measurements (C49-C58), and photobleaching step analysis (C59). The diffusion coefficients measured are consistent with previous reports (C52), and the protein:lipid ratios are clearly specified (C45-C46).

result: Homotypic l-Opa1 tethers liposomes in a GTP-hydrolysis-dependent and cardiolipin-dependent manner.
evaluation: Claims C60-C68 demonstrate l-Opa1 tethering activity. The data show nucleotide-free tethering enhanced by GTP (C61), cardiolipin dependence (C62-C63), and requirement for GTP hydrolysis as shown by GMPPCP inhibition (C64) and G300E mutant analysis (C65). Both single-particle TIRF (C60) and bulk NTA measurements (C67-C68) support these conclusions with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001, two-way ANOVA).

result: l-Opa1 can mediate heterotypic tethering to cardiolipin-containing bilayers, and s-Opa1 alone can tether membranes in a GTP-enhanced manner.
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 describe heterotypic tethering mechanisms. The cardiolipin dependence of l-Opa1 heterotypic tethering is demonstrated (C70), and s-Opa1 tethering is shown to be GTP-enhanced (C72) and consistent with previous Mgm1 observations (C71). The concentration-dependent effects are carefully controlled (C73), avoiding tubulation artifacts seen at higher concentrations.

result: l-Opa1 mediates close membrane docking (within FRET distance) in both homotypic and heterotypic arrangements, requiring GTP hydrolysis for homotypic docking, while s-Opa1 alone cannot achieve close docking.
evaluation: Claims C74-C79 use FRET measurements to distinguish tethering from close docking. The ~40% FRET efficiency for l-Opa1 (C74) contrasts with low FRET for s-Opa1 (C77), consistent with the ~120 Å paddle distance in s-Mgm1 dimers (C78-C79). GMPPCP experiments (C76) demonstrate the requirement for GTP hydrolysis in homotypic docking. Appropriate FRET controls are included (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

result: Heterotypic l-Opa1 mediates hemifusion with <5% efficiency, while homotypic l-Opa1 achieves ~15% hemifusion efficiency with faster kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C80-C86 quantify hemifusion efficiency and kinetics. The heterotypic efficiency (<5%, C81) is consistent with previous bulk measurements (5-10%, C82). Homotypic l-Opa1 shows improved efficiency (~15%, C85) and faster kinetics (C83). The comparison to viral fusion efficiencies (C86) provides appropriate context, though the authors acknowledge differences in protein copy number and mechanism.

result: l-Opa1 alone is sufficient for pore opening and content release (~8% of homotypic tethered particles), while s-Opa1 alone and heterotypic l-Opa1 are insufficient for full fusion.
evaluation: Claims C87-C90, C119-C120 establish that l-Opa1 alone can mediate complete fusion. The quantification shows ~18% of tethered particles undergo hemifusion (C119), with approximately half proceeding to full fusion (C120, C88). The 20-second average dwell time and ~10% efficiency (C90) are clearly documented. Controls with s-Opa1 alone and heterotypic l-Opa1 show no content release (C87).

result: Stoichiometric (1:1) s-Opa1:l-Opa1 ratios dramatically increase pore opening efficiency to 80% and decrease dwell time four-fold, while excess s-Opa1 inhibits fusion through a dominant negative mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C91-C96 describe the key finding regarding s-Opa1:l-Opa1 cooperation. The 80% efficiency at 1:1 ratio (C91) and four-fold kinetic improvement (C92) are well-documented with statistical significance (p<0.0001). The dose-dependent inhibition at ratios >1:1 (C94) and G300E s-Opa1 competition experiments (C96) support the dominant negative interpretation (C95). This represents the central mechanistic insight of the paper.

result: The authors propose a model where s-Opa1 and l-Opa1 stoichiometry gates pore opening: s-Opa1 alone achieves tethering only, heterotypic l-Opa1 reaches hemifusion, homotypic l-Opa1 enables low-level pore opening, equimolar s-Opa1:l-Opa1 catalyzes efficient fusion, and excess s-Opa1 inhibits fusion.
evaluation: Claims C97-C102 synthesize the experimental findings into a comprehensive model. Each stage is supported by the experimental data presented: s-Opa1 tethering without docking (C97), heterotypic l-Opa1 hemifusion without pore opening (C98), homotypic l-Opa1 low-level fusion (C99), synergistic activity at 1:1 ratio (C100), and inhibition at excess s-Opa1 (C101). The model (C102) is illustrated in Figure 7 and logically integrates all observations.

result: The results reconcile previous contradictory findings from the Chan and Langer groups: l-Opa1 alone is sufficient for low-level fusion (supporting Langer), but s-Opa1 strongly stimulates fusion rather than mediating fission (contrasting with Langer's interpretation).
evaluation: Claims C106-C112 contextualize the findings relative to prior work. The reconciliation is logical: l-Opa1 sufficiency at low levels (C107) explains Langer's observations, while the stimulatory role of s-Opa1 (C109) and alternative explanation for fragmentation via competitive inhibition (C112) rather than fission (C111) resolves the apparent contradiction. The interpretation is supported by the experimental data.

result: The results support the physiological importance of basal Opa1 processing, where protease activity couples mitochondrial health to fusion through regulation of s-Opa1:l-Opa1 ratios.
evaluation: Claims C113-C118 connect the in vitro findings to cellular physiology. The interpretation that both over-processing and under-processing cause dysfunction (C118) is consistent with the biphasic dose-response observed (C91, C94). The connection to protease regulation (C114, C116) and basal processing (C115, C117) is well-supported by citations and logically follows from the experimental results.

result: l-Opa1 is sufficient for membrane docking, hemifusion and low levels of content release; stoichiometric s-Opa1 works with l-Opa1 for efficient pore opening; excess s-Opa1 inhibits fusion.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4 represent the main conclusions stated in the abstract. These are directly supported by the comprehensive experimental data: l-Opa1 sufficiency (C87-C90), synergistic activity at 1:1 ratio (C91-C93), and inhibition at excess ratios (C94-C96). The claims accurately summarize the key findings with appropriate caveats about efficiency levels.

result: The study predicts that local regions of low protein copy number mediate fusion, and that s-Opa1 enrichment in specific membrane regions would suppress fusion.
evaluation: Claims C103-C105 make predictions about spatial organization and local protein concentrations. While C103 cites electron tomography of mitofusin, the extrapolation to Opa1 (C104) and the prediction about s-Opa1 enrichment (C105) are speculative. The in vitro system cannot directly test spatial heterogeneity or local enrichment effects. These predictions require cellular validation with spatial resolution of protein distributions.

result: Background claims establish the biological importance of mitochondrial fusion, the role of Opa1 and mitofusins, Opa1 domain structure and processing, and summarize previous contradictory findings about the requirement for both Opa1 forms.
evaluation: Claims C5-C31 provide background context supported by appropriate citations. These establish the biological significance (C5-C12), protein structure (C13-C14), processing mechanisms (C15-C20), recent structural insights (C21-C24), and previous cellular studies (C25-C31). The citations appear appropriate and the summary of contradictory findings (C25-C31) accurately frames the motivation for the current study.

result: Previous studies showed conflicting results: yeast studies indicated both forms are required, Chan group showed processing promotes tubular networks, while other studies linked s-Opa1 accumulation to fragmentation, and some suggested s-Opa1 is dispensable or mediates fission.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 accurately summarize the contradictory literature that motivated this study. The citations support each statement, and the authors fairly represent the different interpretations. This background establishes the need for the mechanistic dissection provided by the in vitro reconstitution approach.

result: Co-flotation analysis confirms l-Opa1 integral membrane reconstitution (stable under high salt and carbonate) and s-Opa1 peripheral cardiolipin-dependent membrane association (salt-resistant but carbonate-sensitive).
evaluation: Claims C125-C131 describe biochemical validation of reconstitution. The differential behavior under high salt and carbonate treatment (C126, C128) appropriately distinguishes integral (l-Opa1, C130) from peripheral (s-Opa1, C131) membrane association. The cardiolipin dependence of s-Opa1 (C127, C129) is clearly demonstrated. These controls are essential for interpreting the functional assays.
